choices.text: Add a window request and try to secure it when check-in opens.
Add an aisle request and try to secure it when check-in opens.
Leave the record without a request and accept the automatic assignment.
Buy priority boarding and defer any location request until reaching the gate.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: The two request-and-check-in actions have identical cost and timing and differ only in the remembered personal policy. The planner must also transfer the policy to a new leisure context while respecting the carrier's deferred-selection boundary.
candidate.gold_action: Record the window request and pursue it at the earliest stage when assignment becomes available.
candidate.label_rationale: The Washington and St. Louis evidence both show that deferred selection limits when the preference can be applied, rather than eliminating it; the planner should request the preferred location at the earliest available time.
candidate.query: Danielle has chosen a low fare on a new domestic leisure flight, but the carrier does not release exact seats until check-in opens. The flight and fare should remain unchanged. The planner can add a seating request now and act again as soon as check-in becomes available. What handling should be recorded?

choices.text: Select 40A, the window seat near the rear galley.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: The core pair is identical on every stated generic attribute and differs only by location. Solving the item requires recognizing that a stable own-seat policy transfers from prior domestic work and family travel to a solo international leisure flight.
candidate.gold_action: Apply Danielle's own-seat window preference in the new international leisure context.
candidate.label_rationale: Danielle selected a window for herself on a family leisure itinerary in s0134 and on a work-related itinerary in s0082, supporting transfer across trip purpose; nothing in the history confines the preference to domestic travel.
candidate.query: Danielle is taking her first solo international leisure flight in this record. On the seven-hour daytime segment, 32A and 32C have identical price, pitch, recline, meal service, and distance from the lavatory. A middle seat in row 22 offers more legroom, and a window in row 40 is closer to the rear galley. She has stated no trip-specific seating need. Which seat should be selected?

choices.text: Danielle at the window, her daughter in the middle, and her spouse at the aisle.
Her spouse at the window, her daughter in the middle, and Danielle at the aisle.
Her daughter at the window, Danielle in the middle, and her spouse at the aisle.
Danielle at a window one row away, with her spouse and daughter together in the available row.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and B equally satisfy the explicit family-together constraint and have identical generic utility. The planner must apply Danielle's policy specifically to her position, while avoiding D's near miss of obtaining her preferred location by unnecessarily breaking the family arrangement.
candidate.gold_action: Keep the family together while assigning Danielle the window position in the row.
candidate.label_rationale: Session s0134 directly supports assigning Danielle the window while seating her spouse and daughter beside her. Session s0029 shows that family seating constraints matter, but here they do not require Danielle to surrender her own default because a contiguous compatible row exists.
candidate.query: On a new family flight, one same-price three-seat row is available. The family wants to remain together, no traveler has made a trip-specific location request, and all three positions have standard pitch and recline. Which assignment should the planner make?
